The letter arrived yesterday, in an envelope that smelled of thyme. “Come before daybreak. I have left the greenhouse door open. You will find what I never managed to explain to the village.” Ada, the keeper of the gardens, always signs her messages with a little drawn leaf. This time, the leaf looks like a waving hand.

You knew her when you were a child: she let you water the tomatoes and never said a question was silly. Then the years passed. You learned of her departure from the neighbours, along with that strange rumour: the old greenhouse was hiding an inheritance Ada refused to sell.

Inside, the morning coolness still holds the night. A watering can waits on a table, a chest occupies the centre of the room and a clock seems to watch over the plants. The glass door at the back leads to the workshop. Ada is not here, but someone has prepared your visit with care.

At the bottom of her letter, she added: “Do not hurry to find the exit. What matters is understanding what you will take with you.”

The greenhouse keeps the small sounds you had forgotten: a drop in a saucer, the rustle of a leaf against glass, the quiet creaking of furniture. Nothing feels like an abandoned place. The tools have been cleaned and the pots watered.

A box bearing your first name sits near the watering can. The central chest is closed with a small brass lock. You look around in vain; no key waits on the nearby hook. On the green cabinet, however, a three-digit combination lock looks recent.

From the outside path, a low voice calls to you. “Are you the person Ada was waiting for? I am Jules, her neighbour. She asked me to stay near the garden until you arrived. She said some things are better understood by discovering them.” Then gravel crunches: he leaves you to explore.

Ada has not turned her house into a trial. She has left you the habits of a craft, precise enough for you to pick up the gestures after her.

The workshop smells of dry earth, wax and paper. The desk is covered with small finished repairs: a sewn handle, a polished shaft, a reglued envelope. Ada cared for objects with the same patience as for plants.

On the shelf, the bottles weigh down a technical sheet. In the centre, a metal box waits under a square of cloth. The wooden door at the back is swollen with damp; a thin coolness escapes from underneath.

The open notebook on the desk recalls an old flood. You were too young to remember it. In the village, people said Ada had closed her gardens after that night. The story seemed simple: too much damage, too little money. Yet the pages show visits, harvests and exchanges throughout all the following years.

Between two leaves, you recognize Jules’s round handwriting. Ada may never have worked as alone as you thought. To understand what they saved together, you will have to go down to where the water used to flow.

A few steps lead down beneath the workshop. Bricks rounded by time outline a passage wide enough for a wheelbarrow. A lamp lights the central valve, and the trickling water gives the place a steady breathing.

To the right, a metal locker has been fixed above the old watermark. At the far end, a staircase climbs back up to the garden. Its upper grate is locked. Beyond it you can see a sky beginning to pale.

An Ada label, well protected from the damp, warns: “This passage is not a shortcut. This is where we understood what deserved to be kept.” The flood left marks, but hands have maintained the place since. The joints are repointed, the steps cleared.

Jules hears you from the other side of the grate. “She made me promise not to give you the answer. But I can tell you this: the chest is not a family treasure. At least, not for a single family.” He urges you to examine the valve before going on.

The grate opens just as daylight touches the last panes of the greenhouse. The garden is not huge. A bench, a fountain and a few flowerbeds are enough to make it feel like a place where you can talk for a long time.

Jules sits near the gate with two cups wrapped in a cloth. “Ada arrived safely at her sister’s, he says. She would have welcomed you herself if she had not been so afraid of changing her mind. She loves this village. Leaving costs her more than she shows.”

You tell him the names from the chest. He nods. “People thought she was keeping rare varieties. Some probably are. But look at the cards: they are mostly meals, voices, moments when someone wanted to thank someone else.”

One last envelope waits for you on the bench. Ada has left you neither an obligation nor a secret to keep to yourself. She has entrusted you with a possibility. Before the gate opens onto the village’s ordinary morning, you still have to give it a shape.
